_meta.title: Ke Aupuni O Ke Akua — Mistranslations Lexicon
_meta.description: Words from the original Biblical Hebrew, Biblical Aramaic, and Koine Greek where common English translations flatten, lose, or invert the descriptive meaning. Every entry keyed by Strong's number. The author field marks which entries are Kahu's own work and which are drafts awaiting his review.
_meta.copyright: © Ke Aupuni O Ke Akua Press. All entries retain copyright.

G25.actual_meaning: To love — but not merely affection or friendship. In classical Greek agapaō meant to be well-pleased, to be contented with. In the NT it carries the weight of a deliberate, self-giving commitment that chooses the well-being of another regardless of response. Distinguished from phileō (emotional fondness) and erōs (desire). God's agapaō of the world (John 3:16) is covenantal, volitional love.
G25.why_mistranslated: Modern English 'love' collapses at least four distinct Greek words into one. The deliberate, covenantal dimension of agapaō is lost — readers hear 'God loved the world' as warm feeling instead of sovereign, committed self-giving.
G25.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G26.actual_meaning: Love — the defining NT word for God's own nature and the command to imitate it. Not sentiment but the steady, purposeful goodwill that seeks the highest good of the beloved. Thayer: 'the deepest and most spiritual of the words for love.' Unlike eros (desire) or philia (friendship/kinship affection), agapē can be commanded because it is a choice, not merely a feeling.
G26.why_mistranslated: English 'love' cannot bear the covenantal weight. Agapē is commandable; feelings are not. Translation collapses this distinction and makes Jesus's commands sound impossible or shallow.
G26.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G932.english_flattened: kingdom (as a place you enter after death)
G932.actual_meaning: Kingdom, reign, royal rule. Not primarily a territory but the active RULE of a king. Basileia tou Theou = the sovereign reign of God breaking into history. Thayer: 'royal power, kingship, dominion, rule.' Jesus uses it almost entirely in the dynamic sense — God's rule arriving, invading, transforming — not a static territory people enter after death.
G932.why_mistranslated: Western political frameworks imported a static 'kingdom-as-place' meaning. Readers hear 'kingdom of heaven' and think of a location rather than the active reign of God breaking in. This single mistranslation has shaped Western Christianity away from Jesus's actual teaching.
G932.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G935.actual_meaning: King — the supreme ruler. In NT context, the title given to God and to Christ as His anointed representative. The word implies absolute sovereign authority, not the constitutional/limited monarchy of modern thought.
G935.why_mistranslated: Modern readers picture ceremonial European monarchs. The NT basileus is war-leader, judge, priest, and representative of the divine rolled into one. The weight of 'Christ is King' is lost when readers hear it through post-Enlightenment monarchy imagery.
G935.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4151.actual_meaning: Spirit, wind, breath. The range of meaning is significant: (1) wind/breath — physical moving air, (2) the animating life-principle in a person, (3) a spiritual being, (4) the Holy Spirit. Context determines which. In John 3:8, Jesus deliberately plays on all the meanings: 'The pneuma blows where it wills... so is everyone born of the pneuma.' The original audience would feel the layered meaning.
G4151.why_mistranslated: 'Ghost' in KJV English now means apparition of the dead. 'Spirit' has become disembodied abstraction. The breath/wind dimension — the same word that describes God's breath in Genesis 2:7 — is lost. Readers miss that Jesus is making a physical pun in John 3.
G4151.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2222.actual_meaning: Life — but specifically the life that belongs to God, divine life, life in its fullest and highest form. Distinguished from bios (G979), which means biological/physical life or livelihood. Zōē aiōnios ('eternal life') does not primarily mean 'life that goes on forever' but 'the life characteristic of the age to come' — God's own quality of life. John uses zōē almost exclusively for this divine, abundant life.
G2222.why_mistranslated: Greek has two words for life (zōē and bios); English has one. The NT's distinction between ordinary biological life and God's own quality of life collapses. 'Eternal life' gets read as duration when the primary meaning is QUALITY — God's kind of life, here now.
G2222.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G165.actual_meaning: Age, era, epoch — a period of time with its own character. NOT simply 'forever.' Aiōnios (the adjective) means 'belonging to the age [to come]' more than 'never-ending.' Thayer: 'a period of time of significant character; the world.' In rabbinic thought there were two ages: ha-olam hazeh (this present age) and ha-olam ha-ba (the age to come). Jesus announced the age to come was arriving.
G165.why_mistranslated: Translating aiōn/aiōnios as 'eternal/forever' imports Greek philosophical ideas of timeless duration. The Hebrew-rooted NT concept is about QUALITY of age, not infinite time. Major theological confusions about 'eternal punishment' and 'eternal life' trace back to this flattening.
G165.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4982.actual_meaning: To save, to rescue, to heal, to make whole. Critically: the word covers healing the sick just as much as rescuing from sin. When Jesus 'saves' someone in the Gospels, the same word is used for both healing the body and forgiving sin — because salvation in the Hebrew/Greek mindset was WHOLENESS, shalom, restoration of the whole person. Not just a ticket to heaven.
G4982.why_mistranslated: Evangelical English narrowed 'saved' to mean 'going to heaven when you die.' The Koine sōzō is holistic: physical healing, social restoration, forgiveness, deliverance from danger. The woman with the bleeding was 'saved' (healed). Blind Bartimaeus was 'saved' (given sight). Collapsing sōzō to eternal salvation loses the gospel's wholeness.
G4982.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G3056.actual_meaning: Word, reason, account, meaning. One of the most theologically loaded words in the NT. In Greek philosophy (Heraclitus, Stoics), Logos was the rational principle ordering the universe. In Jewish thought (Philo), it was the intermediary between God and creation. John 1:1 takes all these layers and says: This Logos is a Person, and He became flesh. The word carries the sense of the articulated mind, the expressed thought, the rational order behind everything.
G3056.why_mistranslated: English 'word' is a label for a spoken sound. Logos is the ORDERING REASON behind reality, the expressed mind of God. When John 1:1 reads 'In the beginning was the Word,' readers hear 'utterance' when they should hear 'the reasoning, ordering intelligence of God made personal.'
G3056.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G5485.actual_meaning: Grace, favor, goodwill. In classical Greek: that which brings joy, a pleasing quality, gratitude. In the NT it becomes the specific word for God's unearned, freely-given favor toward humanity. NOT 'unmerited favor' merely in the sense that we don't deserve it — the Greek carries the additional sense that it flows from the JOYFUL generosity of the giver, not from any calculation of worthiness.
G5485.why_mistranslated: 'Unmerited favor' makes grace transactional — 'I don't deserve it but God gives it anyway.' The Greek is relational: grace flows from God's own joy in giving, not from an assessment of our worthiness. The giver's gladness is the engine.
G5485.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4102.actual_meaning: Faith, trust, faithfulness. This is crucial: pistis is NOT merely intellectual belief. It is the trust that emerges from being persuaded, from evidence. It carries the relational dimension of faithfulness/loyalty (like a treaty). Abraham's pistis was acting on what God said — it was trust that moved his feet. Often translated 'faith' but 'allegiance' or 'covenant loyalty' captures dimensions the English word loses.
G4102.why_mistranslated: Modern English 'faith' has drifted toward 'belief without evidence.' Biblical pistis is trust born from evidence, expressed through loyalty, demonstrated through action. Hebrews 11 is not about sincere belief — it's about people who acted on what God said.
G4102.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H4428.actual_meaning: King. The ancient Near Eastern concept of a king was very different from modern constitutional monarchy. A melek was the military leader, the supreme judge, the high priest's counterpart, and the representative of the divine before the people. In Israel, the earthly melek was always supposed to be subordinate to YHWH, the true Melek. The prophets constantly judged Israel's kings by whether they ruled as YHWH's viceroys or set themselves up as autonomous.
H4428.why_mistranslated: Modern ceremonial-monarch imagery replaces the ancient reality of the king as war-leader, judge, and divine representative. The theological weight of 'YHWH is King' loses its bite when readers imagine a crown and throne instead of sovereign active rule.
H4428.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H4438.actual_meaning: Kingdom, kingship, royal dominion. Like the Greek basileia, this word emphasizes the RULE more than the territory. The Aramaic equivalent malkuta is used in Daniel. In the Kaddish prayer (ancient Jewish liturgy), 'May His kingdom/malkuth come' is the same concept Jesus picks up in the Lord's Prayer — the active, transforming reign of God breaking into human affairs.
H4438.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as basileia. 'Kingdom' in English points to a place; malkuth points to active rule. When the Lord's Prayer says 'thy kingdom come,' Jesus is praying for God's RULE to arrive and transform — not for believers to be transported to a location.
H4438.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H7307.actual_meaning: Spirit, wind, breath. The exact parallel to Greek pneuma. Ruach Elohim in Genesis 1:2 — 'the Spirit/Wind/Breath of God' hovered over the waters. The same word describes the life-giving breath God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7 uses neshamah but ruach carries the same idea). Ezekiel 37: God tells the ruach to breathe into the dry bones. The word is inseparable from life, movement, power, and divine presence.
H7307.why_mistranslated: English has separate words for 'spirit,' 'wind,' and 'breath' — treating them as different categories. Hebrew sees them as one reality. When Genesis says 'the ruach of God moved,' readers miss the layered physicality. God's breath is God's wind is God's Spirit.
H7307.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H2617.actual_meaning: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty, lovingkindness. One of the most untranslatable Hebrew words. No English word captures it alone. BDB: 'goodness, kindness, faithfulness.' It is the love that holds to a covenant even when the other party has broken it. It is YHWH's defining characteristic — the love He showed Israel not because they deserved it but because He committed Himself. Translated 'mercy,' 'lovingkindness,' 'steadfast love,' 'loyalty,' 'grace' in various versions — none is adequate alone.
H2617.why_mistranslated: Every English rendering picks up one dimension and loses the others. 'Mercy' loses the covenant loyalty. 'Lovingkindness' loses the weight. 'Steadfast love' loses the relational commitment. Chesed is all of it at once — and the OT's repeated claim that YHWH's defining characteristic is chesed never lands in English.
H2617.root: possibly related to chasad — to bow down in kindness
H2617.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H6666.actual_meaning: Righteousness, justice — but in the RELATIONAL sense of being in right relationship with others and with God, fulfilling covenant obligations. This is NOT primarily forensic (legal standing) as later Western theology made it. In the OT, tsedaqah means doing right by the poor, the widow, the orphan, the foreigner — it is SOCIAL JUSTICE and COVENANT FAITHFULNESS combined. Abraham 'believed God and it was counted to him as tsedaqah' — meaning he was in right relationship with God.
H6666.why_mistranslated: Western theology (especially post-Reformation) made 'righteousness' mean legal standing before God. The OT meaning is relational and social — doing right by the vulnerable, keeping covenant. When the prophets cry for 'righteousness,' they mean justice for the poor, not individuals attaining moral purity.
H6666.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H7965.actual_meaning: Peace — but the Hebrew concept is FAR richer than the absence of conflict. Shalom is wholeness, completeness, flourishing, right relationships, well-being of the whole person and community. BDB: 'completeness, soundness, welfare, peace.' When the prophets speak of the Prince of Shalom (Isaiah 9:6), they mean the one who will restore total flourishing — economically, relationally, spiritually, physically. The Greek eirēnē (peace) translates it but loses much.
H7965.why_mistranslated: English 'peace' is negative — the absence of war. Shalom is positive — the presence of whole flourishing. The Messianic hope of shalom is not just 'no more fighting' but complete restoration of all things to thriving relationship.
H7965.root: shalem — to be whole, to be complete
H7965.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H1285.actual_meaning: Covenant. The foundational relational-legal concept of the OT. A berith was a solemn binding agreement, usually between unequals, establishing obligations, identity, and relationship. Covenants in the ANE were 'cut' (hence 'cut a covenant') — animals were slaughtered and the parties walked between the pieces, symbolizing: 'may this happen to me if I break these terms.' God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the New Covenant are all berith — God binding Himself to humanity.
H1285.why_mistranslated: Modern 'covenant' sounds like a legal contract or corporate agreement. Berith is relational, blood-sealed, identity-forming. When Scripture says God 'cut a covenant' with Abraham, readers miss the slaughtered animals, the walk between the pieces, the self-curse if the covenant is broken.
H1285.root: uncertain — possibly bara (to cut) or baru (Akkadian: bond)
H1285.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H8451.actual_meaning: Instruction, teaching, direction — not primarily 'law' in the modern legal sense. Torah comes from the verb yarah (to throw, to shoot, to point) — the idea of aiming, directing, teaching the way. The Torah is God's teaching on how to live, not a legal code to be enforced. Psalm 119 loves the Torah as instruction and delight, not as legal burden.
H8451.why_mistranslated: Translating torah as 'law' imports Roman and Enlightenment concepts of statutory legislation. The Hebrew is closer to 'instruction' or 'teaching' — the guidance of a parent or shepherd, not the pronouncement of a court. Paul's critique of 'works of the law' makes different sense when torah means 'instruction' instead of 'legal code.'
H8451.root: yarah — to throw, to shoot, to point
H8451.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H430.actual_meaning: God. The grammatically plural form used with singular verbs when referring to YHWH. In polytheistic contexts it can refer to gods (plural). For Israel: the one God in the fullness of His being. BDB: 'rulers, judges, divine ones, angels, gods, God.' The plural of majesty or fullness — the same pattern as Hebrew mayim (waters) being plural though often singular in meaning. Ancient Jewish and Christian interpreters saw hints of the Trinitarian fullness here.
H430.why_mistranslated: Translating as singular 'God' loses the plural-of-fullness nuance. The grammatical choice matters theologically — elohim with singular verbs preserves both unity and fullness in a way 'God' alone does not.
H430.pos: noun masculine plural (used with singular verbs for the one God)
H430.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3068.actual_meaning: The LORD. The personal covenant name of God, never merely a title. God revealed this name to Moses at the burning bush: 'I AM WHO I AM' / 'I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE' (Exodus 3:14). The name is connected to the Hebrew verb 'to be' — suggesting self-existence, eternal presence, and the God who shows up and acts. Jewish tradition calls this the Tetragrammaton (four letters: YHWH) and considered it too holy to pronounce. English Bibles substitute 'LORD' (all caps) following this tradition.
H3068.why_mistranslated: Substituting 'LORD' turns the personal name into a title. YHWH is to Elohim as 'Philip' is to 'pastor.' When Exodus says 'I am YHWH your Elohim,' it's saying 'I am Yahweh, your God' — name + title. Rendering both as 'the LORD your God' loses the intimate naming that defines covenant relationship.
H3068.root: hayah — to be, to exist, to become
H3068.pos: proper noun — the personal name of God
H3068.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H2421.actual_meaning: To live, to have life, to revive, to give life. This is the root behind chayim (life — always plural in Hebrew, suggesting life in its fullness and multiplicity). BDB: 'to live, to have life, to remain alive, to sustain life, to live prosperously, to revive, to be healed.' In Deuteronomy 30:19, 'choose life' uses this root — it means choose the whole flourishing that comes with covenant faithfulness.
H2421.why_mistranslated: English 'live' means biological survival. Hebrew chayah means flourishing — relational, economic, spiritual, physical thriving. 'Choose life' in Deut 30:19 is not 'avoid death' but 'choose the whole flourishing that covenant with God brings.'
H2421.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3519.actual_meaning: Glory, honor, weight, abundance. The original meaning is HEAVINESS or WEIGHT — what has substance, what is weighty and real. YHWH's kabod is His weighty, substantial, overwhelming presence and splendor. BDB: 'abundance, honor, glory.' When Isaiah says 'the whole earth is full of His glory' (6:3), he means the earth is laden, weighty, full of the presence of God. The NT equivalent is the Greek doxa.
H3519.why_mistranslated: English 'glory' has become religious jargon — vague, ethereal, light-show. Kabod is WEIGHT. Substance. Pressing, undeniable presence. When Moses asked to see God's kabod, he was asking to feel the weight of God's reality. The word teaches a physics of the divine.
H3519.root: kabad — to be heavy, to be weighty
H3519.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

A4437.actual_meaning: Kingdom, royal dominion. The Aramaic equivalent of Hebrew malkuth. Used extensively in Daniel where the shift from Hebrew to Aramaic signals a message for all nations, not just Israel. Daniel's four kingdoms and the 'kingdom of the Most High' (Daniel 7:27) use this word. The Kaddish prayer — which Jesus almost certainly knew — uses malkuth: 'May His kingdom be established.' This is the backdrop for the Lord's Prayer.
A4437.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as Hebrew malkuth and Greek basileia. The Aramaic shifts in Daniel signal a universal message; rendering as static 'kingdom' obscures both the rule/reign emphasis and the cross-linguistic continuity.
A4437.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

A426.actual_meaning: God. The Aramaic form of the Hebrew El/Elohim. Used in Daniel and Ezra where those books shift to Aramaic. Nebuchadnezzar uses this word when he recognizes God after his madness (Daniel 4:2). The same root appears in the Arabic Allah.
A426.why_mistranslated: Translating simply as 'God' loses the cross-Semitic continuity. Elah, Eloah, Elohim, Allah — all share the same Semitic root for deity. When Daniel's pagan kings recognize 'the God of heaven,' the shared-root word carries weight that a bare English 'God' cannot.
A426.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2212.english_flattened: seek (find it once and you are done)
G2212.actual_meaning: To seek — but in the present imperative tense the action never stops. Picture a woman who has lost a coin and turns her whole house upside down, moving every piece of furniture, sweeping every corner, until she finds it. That is what Jesus is commanding in Matthew 6:33. Keep seeking. Keep pursuing. Do not stop until the Kingdom of God is the organizing direction of your entire life. The present tense in Koine carries continuous, unending action — a lifestyle command, not a one-time task.
G2212.why_mistranslated: English 'seek' sounds like a single event — you seek, you find, you move on. The Koine present imperative is a lifetime direction. Jesus is not giving a task to complete. He is describing the posture of your whole life.
G2212.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1525.actual_meaning: To enter INTO the experience of something — not merely cross a threshold. You can walk into a gym and never touch a weight. You entered the building but not the experience of training. When Jesus says in Matthew 18:3 that you must enter the Kingdom like a child, He is not talking about getting through a gate when you die. He is talking about entering INTO the living experience of God's reign — being reshaped by it, humbled by it, transformed by it right now. The composite eis (into) + erchomai (to come) describes immersion, not admission.
G1525.why_mistranslated: English 'enter' is a boundary word — you cross a line and you are in. The Koine is an immersion word. This one mistranslation turned the gospel of transformation into a gospel of admission. People spend their lives asking 'will I get in?' when Jesus was asking 'are you experiencing the Kingdom now?'
G1525.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G3340.actual_meaning: To completely change direction — in your mind and your life. Meta means change, noeō means to think and perceive. A man walking toward a cliff who turns completely around and walks the other way — that is metanoeō. When John the Baptist and Jesus both opened their ministry with this word, they were not asking people to cry. They were saying: everything you have been walking toward, turn away from it, because God's Kingdom is arriving and you need to face the right direction to receive it.
G3340.why_mistranslated: The Latin Vulgate translated this as 'do penance.' That single decision shaped a thousand years of Western Christianity into guilt, confession rituals, and emotional sorrow. The Koine word has no tears in it. It has a change of direction.
G3340.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G3340_name.actual_meaning: A complete reorientation of mind and life direction. The noun form of metanoeō. Not an emotion — a turning. The Hebrew equivalent is shuv, which means to turn around and walk back. Repentance in the Biblical sense is not feeling bad about where you have been. It is changing the direction you are heading. Paul distinguishes in 2 Corinthians 7:10 between godly metanoia that leads to life and worldly sorrow that leads only to death. The sorrow is not the repentance — the turning is.
G3340_name.why_mistranslated: Same Latin penance problem as metanoeō. The church made repentance into an emotional and ritual transaction. The Scripture makes it a directional one.
G3340_name.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1577.english_flattened: church (a building, a denomination, a Sunday service)
G1577.actual_meaning: The called-out assembly. In the Greek world, the ekklēsia was the civic assembly of a city — citizens called out of their homes to gather and govern their community together. It was a political, community word about people exercising their shared identity. When Jesus said 'I will build my ekklēsia' in Matthew 16:18, He was not talking about constructing a building. He was describing a gathered people called out of the old order into the new one — the citizens of the Kingdom, assembled and functioning together.
G1577.why_mistranslated: The English word 'church' comes from kuriakon, meaning a building belonging to the Lord. Somewhere in translation history, the word for the gathered people got replaced by the word for the building they sometimes meet in. Most Christians now think church is a place you go instead of a people you are.
G1577.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1343.actual_meaning: Right relationship — with God, with other people, with the created world. The Greek equivalent of Hebrew tsedaqah, carrying the same relational weight. It is not primarily about your personal moral record. It is about being in right standing with the people around you, keeping covenant, doing right by the poor and the vulnerable. When Jesus in Matthew 6:33 says seek His dikaiosynē, He means seek the right-ordering of all relationships the way God intends — justice flowing like water, the broken restored.
G1343.why_mistranslated: Post-Reformation theology made righteousness a legal verdict — your standing before the court of God. The relational and social dimension was largely lost. When the prophets cried out for righteousness, they were not asking people to have better devotional lives. They were demanding that the poor be treated justly.
G1343.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G40.english_flattened: holy (morally perfect, untouched by the world)
G40.actual_meaning: Set apart. Dedicated. Different by design. Holiness in the Greek is not first about moral perfection — it is about being in a distinct category, consecrated for a specific purpose. The ground at the burning bush was hagios not because it had better soil but because God was present there and had set it apart. When Paul addresses all believers as hagioi — saints, holy ones — he is not saying they achieved moral perfection. He is saying they have been set apart, called out, designated for God's purposes.
G40.why_mistranslated: English 'holy' has come to mean impossibly pure and morally flawless. This makes 'be holy as I am holy' sound like a crushing impossibility. The Koine reading makes it an identity statement — you are set apart, live from that reality.
G40.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H6918.actual_meaning: Set apart. Separate. Categorically different. YHWH is qadosh because He is utterly unlike everything else in existence. When the seraphim cry qadosh, qadosh, qadosh in Isaiah 6, they are not announcing that God has passed a moral test. They are declaring that He is beyond all comparison — incomparably other, absolutely distinct. When Israel is called to be a qadosh nation, they are called to live visibly different from the nations around them — not better in pride but distinct in purpose, shaped by YHWH's character.
H6918.why_mistranslated: Making qadosh mean moral perfection turns holiness into a standard no one can reach and makes God's holiness into a wall between Him and humanity rather than the description of His incomparable nature.
H6918.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G266.english_flattened: sin (breaking God's rules, committing a crime against God)
G266.actual_meaning: Missing the mark. This is an archery word. When an arrow is released and fails to reach the target, that is hamartia. Human beings were made for a target — to bear the image of God, to live in covenant relationship, to flourish the way God designed. Sin is anything that misses that target: rebellion, ignorance, weakness, drift. It is not primarily a crime against a legal code. It is a failure to hit what we were made for. That difference changes everything about what salvation means.
G266.why_mistranslated: When sin is a legal category, salvation becomes a legal solution — the penalty is paid, the record is cleared. When sin is missing the mark, salvation becomes restoration — the person is retrained, the aim is corrected, the life is reoriented toward its true purpose.
G266.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G3788.actual_meaning: Eye — but in the Jewish world behind the Koine, the eye described the character of a person's heart. A good eye meant a generous, open-handed, single-focused person. A bad eye meant a stingy, envious, grasping person. When Jesus teaches about the lamp of the body being the eye in Matthew 6:22-23, He is speaking into a Hebrew idiom His audience knew: the way you see the world — with generosity or with envy, with single focus or with divided loyalty — determines whether your whole life is full of light or darkness.
G3788.why_mistranslated: Reading eye as a physical organ turns this passage into mystical obscurity. Reading it through the Jewish idiom it was spoken from reveals a sharp and practical teaching about the posture of the heart toward God and toward people.
G3788.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2889.english_flattened: world (the planet Earth, or all humanity)
G2889.actual_meaning: An ordered system — the arrangement of human civilization around values, priorities, and powers that stand in opposition to God's Kingdom. Kosmos originally meant order, arrangement, the opposite of chaos. By NT times it described both the created order and the system of human society organized around wealth, status, power, and self rather than God. When John says do not love the kosmos (1 John 2:15), he does not mean hate the earth or hate people. He means do not be shaped by the value system of the age. When Jesus says God loved the kosmos (John 3:16), He means the people caught inside that broken system.
G2889.why_mistranslated: Flattening kosmos to mean the earth or all people loses the systemic critique central to NT theology. John is not asking for earth-hatred. He is asking for resistance to the invisible ordering of life that pulls people away from God.
G2889.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4561.english_flattened: flesh (the physical body, which is sinful by nature)
G4561.actual_meaning: Human life organized around the self, apart from God. Paul uses sarx as a theological term — not a verdict against the physical body. He calls the body a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19) and says God will raise it from the dead. Sarx is the mode of existence in which a person lives by their own strength, trusts their own wisdom, and pursues their own agenda. Self-reliant humanity. That is what is crucified with Christ — not the body, but the self-first way of living.
G4561.why_mistranslated: Reading sarx as the sinful physical body has caused enormous damage — body shame, contempt for physical life, the idea that becoming more spiritual means becoming less embodied. Paul is not a Greek philosopher who thinks matter is evil. He thinks self-first living is the problem and Spirit-led living is the solution.
G4561.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G5590.english_flattened: soul (an immortal spiritual substance trapped in the body)
G5590.actual_meaning: Life. Self. The whole living person. Genesis 2:7 says God breathed into Adam and he became a living nephesh — the Greek LXX translates that as living psychē. The psychē is not a detachable part of you that floats free when the body dies. It is you — breathing, feeling, choosing, the whole embodied self that God made and called good. When Jesus says whoever loses his psychē for my sake will find it, He means whoever gives up their whole life will discover what life actually is.
G5590.why_mistranslated: Plato taught that the soul was immortal and trapped in the body, and death was the soul's liberation. This crept into Christian theology and changed psychē from the whole living person into an immortal spiritual fragment. The result is a Christianity shaped more by Greek philosophy than Hebrew Scripture.
G5590.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1391.english_flattened: glory (vague spiritual brightness, a light show)
G1391.actual_meaning: Weight. Substance. The undeniable, pressing presence of God's reality. Doxa is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew kabod — which literally means heaviness. When Moses asked to see God's glory, he was asking to feel the weight of God's reality bearing down on him. When Isaiah says the whole earth is full of His glory, he means the earth is saturated with God's substantial, weighty presence. When John says we beheld His glory in John 1:14, he means they felt the press of who Jesus actually was — the full substance of God in human flesh, impossible to ignore.
G1391.why_mistranslated: Modern worship has trained people to think of glory as atmosphere or lighting. The Scripture means something far more physical — a weight, a substance, an overwhelming press of divine reality that cannot be dismissed.
G1391.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2347.actual_meaning: Pressure. Squeezing. The physical sensation of being compressed. Thlipsis comes from pressing grapes or crushing olives — things squeezed until what is inside comes out under pressure. In the NT it describes the present, ongoing experience of following Jesus in a world that has not yet submitted to His rule. Jesus says in John 16:33 you will have thlipsis in this world — not 'you will face a future event' but 'the pressure of living as Kingdom citizens in a world organized against the Kingdom is something you feel right now, every day.'
G2347.why_mistranslated: End-times theology attached the word tribulation almost entirely to a future prophetic timeline. Millions of Christians now look for thlipsis on a calendar while missing the daily pressure they are already under — and missing the strength that pressure is building in them.
G2347.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G40_pneuma_agion.actual_meaning: The Set-Apart Breath. The Set-Apart Wind. Pneuma is breath and wind — physical, life-giving, moving. Hagion means set apart, consecrated. The Holy Spirit is the dedicated Breath of God — the same Breath that moved over the waters in Genesis 1:2, that God exhaled into Adam's nostrils in Genesis 2:7, that filled the room at Pentecost like a mighty rushing wind in Acts 2. There is nothing ghostly about it. It is the living, breathing presence of God, moving like wind, giving life like breath.
G40_pneuma_agion.why_mistranslated: In 1611, 'ghost' still meant spirit or breath. In modern English, ghost means the restless dead. Every generation raised on Holy Ghost hears something haunted when they should hear something alive and powerful.
G40_pneuma_agion.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G863.actual_meaning: To send away. To release. To let go. The word is built from apo (from, away) + hiēmi (to send). When Jesus forgives sins, He sends them away — dismisses them, releases them, sets the person free from their weight. The same word is used for releasing a debt, dismissing a crowd, letting go of a grudge. It is not a courtroom word. It is a releasing word. When Jesus teaches His disciples to forgive as they have been forgiven, He is asking them to actively release — to open their hands and let go.
G863.why_mistranslated: Translating aphiēmi as a legal pardon makes forgiveness sound like a transaction — the penalty is cancelled, the record is adjusted. The Koine is more physical — the thing is sent away, released, no longer held. The difference matters: a pardon leaves the crime on record. A releasing lets it go completely.
G863.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2098.english_flattened: gospel (the religious message of how to get saved and go to heaven)
G2098.actual_meaning: Royal good news — specifically the kind of announcement made when a new king took the throne or a great military victory was won. Eu (good) + angelion (announcement). In the Roman world, euangelion was the official proclamation of imperial news. When NT writers call the message of Jesus the euangelion, they are deliberately using the language of empire — and saying that Jesus, not Caesar, is the true King. 'The euangelion of Jesus Christ, the Son of God' is a political declaration: there is a new ruler, and His name is not Caesar.
G2098.why_mistranslated: Reducing gospel to a private religious message about individual salvation after death strips out the cosmic and political dimensions. The early Christians who were fed to lions were not killed for having a private religious belief. They were killed for declaring that Jesus is Lord — which meant Caesar is not.
G2098.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1401.english_flattened: servant (a paid employee or hired helper)
G1401.actual_meaning: Slave. Bondservant. Someone who is owned, not hired. A doulos had no legal rights of their own, no separate agenda, belonged entirely to their master. When Paul opens his letter to the Romans by calling himself doulos of Christ Jesus, he is not saying he has a job working for Jesus. He is saying he belongs entirely to Jesus — his time, his agenda, his life, all of it. This is the language of total belonging, not employment.
G1401.why_mistranslated: Translators softened doulos to servant to avoid the discomfort of the word slave. But Paul chose this word deliberately. The total-belonging it describes is exactly what he means. Softening it to servant makes discipleship sound like a part-time arrangement.
G1401.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2962.english_flattened: Lord (a polite religious title, like calling someone sir)
G2962.actual_meaning: Master. Owner. The one who holds absolute authority. In the Roman world, kyrios was the title of the emperor — Caesar is kyrios. Jewish writers used it in the LXX to translate the divine name YHWH. When the early Christians confessed that Jesus is kyrios, they were making two claims simultaneously: Jesus is the divine YHWH, and Jesus is the true Emperor over against Caesar's false claim. It was not a polite religious honorific. In the Roman empire it was a treasonous statement.
G2962.why_mistranslated: The word Lord has become so domesticated in church culture that it has lost its edge entirely. Hymnals and prayers have turned it into a reverent but harmless title. The Koine word got people killed. Recovering its weight recovers the actual claim of the gospel.
G2962.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G3813.english_flattened: little child (someone innocent, simple, and pure-hearted)
G3813.actual_meaning: A young child — but in the honor culture of Jesus's day, children had essentially zero social status. They were at the bottom of the hierarchy, completely dependent, with no rights and no voice. When Jesus says unless you become as paidia you cannot enter the Kingdom (Matthew 18:3), He is not asking you to be innocent or simple. He is asking you to take the lowest place. To release every claim to status, honor, and position. To stand before God with the radical dependence of someone who has nothing to offer and no standing to negotiate from.
G3813.why_mistranslated: Western sentimentality reads children as symbols of innocence and purity. In the first-century Mediterranean world, children were symbols of low status and total dependence. Jesus is making a far sharper demand than asking people to be sweet and uncomplicated.
G3813.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H7225.actual_meaning: Beginning, yes — but also the chief thing, the principal thing, the first and best. The root is rosh, meaning head. Reshith is not just when something started — it is what stands at the head, what has primacy. In Genesis 1:1, bereshith carries both meanings: at the start, and as the principal act. In Proverbs 1:7, the fear of YHWH is the reshith of knowledge — not merely the first step but the most important thing, the head of all wisdom. When you bring the reshith of your harvest, you bring the first and the best, not just the earliest.
H7225.why_mistranslated: Translating reshith only as beginning loses the primacy and rank dimension entirely. The word teaches that what comes first also matters most — not just chronologically but in value and weight.
H7225.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H1254.english_flattened: create (make something, the way humans make things)
H1254.actual_meaning: To create — a verb used in the Hebrew Bible exclusively with God as the subject. No human ever baras. Humans asah (make, do) and yatsar (form, shape). Bara is reserved for what only God does — bringing into being what did not exist, accomplishing what no creature can accomplish. Genesis 1:1 uses bara for the cosmos. Genesis 1:27 uses it for humanity. Isaiah uses it for God's new work in history. The exclusivity of the word is its entire point.
H1254.why_mistranslated: English create is used freely for human and divine activity alike. We say an artist creates a painting. The Hebrew never says that. Flattening bara into generic creating erases the line Scripture draws between what God does and what creatures do.
H1254.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H5315.english_flattened: soul (an immortal spiritual substance separate from and superior to the body)
H5315.actual_meaning: Life. Self. The whole living creature. Genesis 2:7 says God breathed into Adam and he became a living nephesh — not he received a soul, but he became a living being, whole. Animals are also called nephesh in Genesis 1:20. The nephesh is not a detachable inner part. It is the whole person breathing and alive. When the Psalms say bless YHWH O my nephesh, David is not addressing a spiritual fragment. He is calling his whole living self to attention before God.
H5315.why_mistranslated: Same Platonic contamination as psychē. The idea of an immortal soul trapped in a mortal body is Greek philosophy, not Hebrew Scripture. Hebrew anthropology sees the person as a whole — body, breath, life, all one. The Christian hope is not the soul escaping the body. It is the resurrection of the whole person.
H5315.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H2403.english_flattened: sin (a moral crime, a rule broken)
H2403.actual_meaning: Missing the mark. The Hebrew equivalent of the Greek hamartia — the same archery picture. From the root chata, to miss, to fail to reach. The word also names the sin-offering in the sacrificial system — meaning the word carries both the failure and the remedy in the same breath. The whole sacrificial system makes more sense when sin is missing the mark of covenant faithfulness — the offerings are the means of restoring aim, not of paying a criminal penalty.
H2403.why_mistranslated: Same as hamartia. Making chattath primarily a legal violation shapes the entire OT sacrificial system into a punishment system. Understanding it as missing the mark shapes the same system into a restoration system. The theology of atonement changes depending on which picture you hold.
H2403.root: chata — to miss, to fail to reach
H2403.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3722.english_flattened: atone (appease an angry God with a sacrifice)
H3722.actual_meaning: To cover. To wipe away. To cleanse. The root idea is removing or covering defilement — not appeasing an angry deity. The mercy seat in the tabernacle is the kapporeth — the covering place, the cleansing place. Kaphar is covenant maintenance: when something has marred the relationship between God and His people, kaphar removes the defilement so the relationship can continue. The emphasis is on cleansing, not on paying a penalty to calm divine wrath.
H3722.why_mistranslated: Popular Christianity often frames atonement as appeasing an angry God — a picture closer to pagan sacrifice than to Hebrew covenant theology. Kaphar is about cleaning, not calming. God is not a volatile deity who needs to be managed. He is a covenant partner whose relationship with His people is being actively maintained.
H3722.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H6944.actual_meaning: Set-apartness. Consecration. Dedicated distinctness. The noun form of qadosh. The holy of holies — qodesh qadashim — is the most dedicated space, the place most fully set apart for YHWH's presence. Israel as a holy nation is a set-apart nation — distinct from the others not in arrogance but in purpose, shaped by YHWH's character and living visibly differently as a result.
H6944.why_mistranslated: Same as qadosh. Moral perfection as the meaning of holiness makes it an achievement — something you attain. Set-apartness as the meaning makes it an identity — something you live from. The call to holiness in Scripture is a call to live from who you already are in God, not to earn a status you do not have.
H6944.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3372.actual_meaning: To revere. To stand in awe. To take with full seriousness. When the OT says fear YHWH, it does not mean cower before an unpredictable deity. It means respond rightly to who God actually is — His weight, His reality, His covenant claims. The person who fears YHWH is not paralyzed with terror. They are the person who takes God seriously enough to let that reality shape every decision. Proverbs 1:7 calls this the reshith — the principal thing — of all wisdom.
H3372.why_mistranslated: Translating yare as simple terror has produced a picture of God as someone to be appeased and avoided. But Scripture constantly follows 'fear not' with 'I am with you' — because the yare YHWH is not about cringing. It is about the posture of a creature standing before the Creator with appropriate reverence and trust.
H3372.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3045.english_flattened: know (to have information about someone or something)
H3045.actual_meaning: To know through relationship, through experience, through intimate encounter. This is the word used for the sexual union between Adam and Eve — Adam knew his wife and she conceived. It is knowing through lived encounter, not through accumulated facts. When God says I knew you before you were formed in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5), He is not talking about having data about Jeremiah. He is speaking of the deep relational knowing of a covenant partner. When Jesus says I never knew you (Matthew 7:23), He means we never had relationship.
H3045.why_mistranslated: English know has drifted almost entirely toward informational knowing — I know the facts about you. Hebrew yada is relational knowing — I have encountered you, lived with you, been changed by you. When Jesus in John 17:3 says eternal life is knowing the Father, He means relationship, not theology.
H3045.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H5650.actual_meaning: Slave. Bondservant. Owned, not hired. The Hebrew equivalent of the Greek doulos. Moses is called eved YHWH — slave of YHWH. David is called eved YHWH. This is the highest honor the OT bestows on a human being — to belong wholly to God, to have no separate agenda, to be entirely at His disposal. It is total belonging described as dignity, not as degradation.
H5650.why_mistranslated: Same softening as doulos. The total-belonging dimension that makes the title meaningful is lost when it becomes a mere job description. When the prophets speak of the Servant of YHWH in Isaiah, they are describing someone whose entire existence is organized around YHWH's purposes — not someone who does occasional tasks for God.
H5650.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3467.actual_meaning: To deliver. To rescue. To bring into a wide, safe space. The root idea is making room — bringing someone out of a tight, dangerous place into spaciousness and safety. Yasha is the root of the name Yeshua — YHWH saves, YHWH delivers. In the OT, yasha describes rescue from real, concrete danger: enemies, famine, oppression, sickness. When Gabriel tells Joseph to name the child Yeshua because He will yasha His people from their sins, the word carries its full concrete rescue weight — not a future spiritual transaction but a real deliverance from the most fundamental danger human beings face.
H3467.why_mistranslated: Evangelical English narrowed salvation to mean going to heaven when you die. Hebrew yasha is wholeness rescue — political, economic, physical, spiritual, relational. The same word saves Israel from Egypt, heals the sick, and delivers the oppressed. Salvation in Hebrew thought is shalom breaking in now.
H3467.root: y-sh-a — to be wide, to make room, to deliver
H3467.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H5414.english_flattened: give (transfer ownership with no strings attached)
H5414.actual_meaning: To give — but in the Hebrew worldview, a gift from God is never a detached transfer. Nathan carries relational weight: to give, to appoint, to entrust, to set in place for a purpose. When God nathans the land to Israel, it comes with covenant obligations. When God nathans a gift, He remains present in the gift. Gifts in Hebrew thought carry the giver's claim and the receiver's responsibility. This is why Paul says in Romans 11:29 that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable — they were not transactions, they were covenant commitments.
H5414.why_mistranslated: English give has become entirely transactional — ownership changes hands and the giver steps back. Hebrew nathan keeps the giver present and engaged. This changes how we understand every gift God has given — land, Torah, covenant, salvation. All of them come with the Giver still in the picture.
H5414.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H5769.actual_meaning: An age stretching beyond the horizon of sight. The root idea is hidden — that which is so far off it passes out of view. Like the Greek aiōn, olam refers to an age with its own character, not to mathematical infinity. The two-age framework of Hebrew thought — ha-olam ha-zeh (this present age) and ha-olam ha-ba (the age to come) — uses olam for both ages. When Psalm 90:2 says from olam to olam YHWH is God, it means from age to age, from before time began to beyond where time ends — not from mathematical past infinity to mathematical future infinity.
H5769.why_mistranslated: Translating olam as forever imports Greek philosophical infinity into a Hebrew relational word. The difference matters enormously for understanding passages about eternal life, eternal punishment, and the everlasting covenant — all of which are about the quality and character of the age to come, not about endless duration.
H5769.root: a-l-m — to hide, to be hidden
H5769.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H4872_name.english_flattened: Moses (just a name, no meaning carried)
H4872_name.actual_meaning: Drawn out. Given by Pharaoh's daughter when she pulled the infant from the water — she called him Mosheh, saying, I drew him out of the water. But the name is prophetic in both directions. Moses was drawn out of the water as an infant, and decades later he drew Israel out through the water of the Red Sea. His name carries his entire life's mission. In Hebrew, names describe. Pharaoh's daughter spoke over this child, without knowing it, the shape of his whole life.
H4872_name.why_mistranslated: In English, Moses is just a proper name — a label. In Hebrew, every time his name is spoken it tells the story of who he is and what he was born to do. This is how Hebrew names function throughout Scripture. The name carries the person.
H4872_name.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3478_name.english_flattened: Israel (the name of a nation, no meaning carried)
H3478_name.actual_meaning: He who wrestles with God — or God who prevails. Given to Jacob after he spent the night wrestling with the angel at the Jabbok river and would not let go until he received a blessing (Genesis 32:28). The name describes the defining characteristic of the whole people: a community whose relationship with God is marked by honest struggle, persistent engagement, refusal to let go. Not passive compliance. Not easy agreement. Wrestling — and being changed by the wrestling.
H3478_name.why_mistranslated: Treating Israel as merely a national label loses the theological identity embedded in the name. Every time the name is spoken in Scripture it carries the Jabbok story — a people defined by their willingness to engage God honestly, to hold on through the night, to demand blessing even when it costs them.
H3478_name.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2424_name.english_flattened: Jesus (just a first name, no meaning carried)
G2424_name.actual_meaning: YHWH saves. YHWH delivers. The Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua — which is itself a sentence: the covenant name of God plus the verb yasha, to save. Every time the name is spoken it declares who He is and what He does. Gabriel's instruction to Joseph in Matthew 1:21 is built entirely on this — you shall call His name Yeshua, for He will yasha His people from their sins. The name and the mission are the same word.
G2424_name.why_mistranslated: Translating through Greek to Latin to English has buried the living sentence inside a sound. To Hebrew ears, Yeshua announced His purpose every time it was spoken. English speakers have a name. Hebrew speakers had a declaration.
G2424_name.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G5547.actual_meaning: The Anointed One. Messiah. This is not a surname — it is a royal title carrying centuries of covenant promise. The Greek translation of the Hebrew Mashiach — the anointed king promised to David, the anointed prophet, the anointed priest. Jesus Christ means Yeshua the Anointed King. When Paul says Jesus is the Christos, he is making the claim that got people killed in the Roman world: the one YHWH anointed to rule has arrived, and His throne supersedes every other.
G5547.why_mistranslated: Treating Christ as a last name has quietly stripped one of the most loaded titles in Scripture of all its meaning. Most people who say Jesus Christ are unwittingly saying Jesus Smith. Recovering the title recovers the claim — He is not just a religious figure, He is the Anointed King promised since David.
G5547.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4341.english_flattened: worship (sing songs, attend services, express religious feeling)
G4341.actual_meaning: To fall face-down before someone in complete submission and reverence. Literally to kiss toward — the physical act of prostrating yourself before a king or deity. Proskyneō is full-body, floor-level humility. When the magi arrived and proskyneō'd the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11), they physically fell on their faces. When the 24 elders proskyneō in Revelation, they fall down from their thrones. This is not singing. It is the posture of a creature acknowledging total sovereignty.
G4341.why_mistranslated: Contemporary worship culture has reduced proskyneō to an emotional and musical experience. The word is a bodily posture — the whole self laid low before the one who is actually Lord. When worship becomes only music and feeling, the physical dimension of surrender that the word demands is quietly lost.
G4341.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G3870.english_flattened: comfort (console someone who is sad) OR beseech (weakly beg)
G3870.actual_meaning: To call alongside. Para (beside) + kaleō (to call). The word covers several related ideas that all share the same core picture: someone is called to come alongside another person for a specific purpose. It can mean comfort — calling someone to stand with you in your pain. It can mean exhort — calling someone strongly to a course of action. It can mean urge — pressing someone with conviction toward something important. The Holy Spirit is called the Paraklētos — the One called to stand alongside — which means helper, advocate, comforter, and guide all at once.
G3870.why_mistranslated: English splits parakaleo into comfort and beseech as if they were different words. They are the same word — the range of meaning is the point. Whenever God draws alongside a person, the result could be consolation, challenge, or both at the same time.
G3870.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G26_phileo.english_flattened: love (identical to agapaō — just another word for love)
G26_phileo.actual_meaning: To love with natural affection, warmth, and friendship. The love of kinship, of familiarity, of emotional closeness. Different from agapaō, which is willed, covenantal, chosen love. In John 21, the distinction between these two words carries the entire weight of the scene. Jesus asks Peter twice using agapaō — do you love me with covenant commitment? Peter answers both times with phileō — I love you like a brother. The third time Jesus meets Peter where he is and asks using phileō — do you love me as a friend? The whole conversation is a masterwork of pastoral grace visible only in the Greek.
G26_phileo.why_mistranslated: English has one word for love and flattens both Greek words into it. The John 21 dialogue — one of the most tender exchanges in Scripture — becomes impossible to follow in English translation. Peter is not being inconsistent or evasive. He is being honest about where his faith actually is, and Jesus is meeting him there.
G26_phileo.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2588.english_flattened: heart (the seat of emotion and feeling)
G2588.actual_meaning: The center of the whole inner life — thinking, willing, and feeling together. In the biblical worldview, the heart is where decisions are made, where trust is placed, where the direction of a life is set. It is not just the emotional center. It thinks — out of the heart come evil thoughts (Matthew 15:19). It believes — with the heart one trusts (Romans 10:9-10). It chooses — set your heart on things above (Colossians 3:1). The command to love God with all your kardia means engage your whole deciding, willing, trusting inner self — not merely feel warmly.
G2588.why_mistranslated: Modern Western culture split head from heart — thinking from feeling. Biblical thought keeps them together. The heart in Scripture is the command center of the whole person. When this is lost, every command that touches the heart gets reduced to an emotional appeal.
G2588.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3820.actual_meaning: The center of all inner life — thinking, deciding, willing, feeling, all in one. Hebrew anthropology does not split intellect from emotion. The leb is where a person processes reality and chooses a direction. Wisdom enters the leb (Proverbs 2:10). The deceitful leb reasons its way into trouble (Jeremiah 17:9). God searches the leb to know what a person is actually doing with their life (1 Samuel 16:7). When Proverbs says guard your leb above all else (4:23), it is not asking you to manage your emotions. It is asking you to protect the decision-making center of your whole life.
H3820.why_mistranslated: Same split as kardia. Making leb primarily emotional makes Scripture's constant address to the heart sound like emotional management advice. The Hebrew is governance advice — the leb steers the whole person, and what enters it shapes everything downstream.
H3820.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1411.actual_meaning: Inherent ability — the power that belongs to something by its very nature. The root of the English words dynamite and dynamic. Dynamis is not borrowed or given power. It is built-in capacity. When Jesus felt dynamis go out from Him when the woman touched His robe (Luke 8:46), it was His own inherent divine ability flowing outward in response to her faith. When Paul says the gospel is the dynamis of God for salvation (Romans 1:16), he means the gospel has built-in capacity to do what it says — it carries the power of transformation within itself.
G1411.why_mistranslated: English power covers too much territory — it can mean political power, muscle, electricity, or influence. Dynamis is specifically the inherent, nature-given capacity of a thing to accomplish what it was made for. The gospel does not need external reinforcement. Its dynamis is already inside it.
G1411.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1849.actual_meaning: Delegated authority. The right to act. Jurisdiction. Different from dynamis, which is inherent ability. Exousia is authorized power — permission and the right to exercise dominion in a specific domain. When Jesus gives His disciples exousia over unclean spirits (Mark 6:7), He is deputizing them — transferring His authority to act in His name. When He declares all exousia has been given to Him (Matthew 28:18), He is claiming delegated throne-authority from the Father. Exousia is the right. Dynamis is the ability. You need both.
G1849.why_mistranslated: Translating both exousia and dynamis as power erases a distinction the NT writers made carefully. In the Great Commission, Jesus grounds the mission in exousia — delegated authority from the throne. That is a different foundation than emotional enthusiasm or personal ability.
G1849.root: exesti — it is permitted, it is lawful
G1849.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2983.english_flattened: receive (passively wait for something to be given to you)
G2983.actual_meaning: To take. To lay hold of. To actively grasp. Lambanō is not passive reception — it is active taking. When John 1:12 says as many as received Him, the word means those who actively took hold of Him, who laid hold of what was being offered and grasped it. When Jesus says receive the Holy Spirit in John 20:22, He is not describing something that will happen to passive recipients. He is calling for an active taking hold of the Breath being offered.
G2983.why_mistranslated: English receive has become almost entirely passive — you receive a gift, meaning it is handed to you and you stand there with your hands open. Lambanō is active grasping. The picture of salvation and of receiving the Spirit as passive waiting has shaped generations of believers into consumers of spiritual experience rather than active participants.
G2983.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4100.actual_meaning: To trust. To rely upon. To stake your life on. The verb form of pistis. Biblical pisteuō is not mental assent to a list of facts — it is the trust that moves your feet. Abraham pisteuō'd God and it was counted as righteousness — meaning he packed up everything he owned and left for a land he had never seen. That is not mental agreement. That is a life reorganized around trust. James makes the same point in reverse: the demons pisteuō in one God and tremble. Mental agreement without life-change is not what Scripture calls faith.
G4100.why_mistranslated: Modern English believe has been weakened to mean 'accept as true in the mind.' Pisteuō is whole-life trust. The altar call question 'do you believe?' when it means 'do you mentally agree?' is asking a far smaller question than Jesus asked His disciples when He said follow me.
G4100.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2476.actual_meaning: To stand firm. To be established. To hold your ground. Histēmi carries the sense of being rooted and fixed in a position — not merely being vertical. When Paul tells believers to stand in Ephesians 6:11-13, using the word three times in three verses, he is not talking about posture. He is describing the established, planted, unmovable position of someone who has taken their ground in Christ and will not be moved from it regardless of what comes against them.
G2476.why_mistranslated: Reading histēmi as simply being upright turns the armor of God passage into instructions for not falling over. The Koine is about holding your established position against everything that would displace you from it. The emphasis is on rootedness, not on verticality.
G2476.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H7725.english_flattened: return (come back to a place you left)
H7725.actual_meaning: Turn around. Reverse direction. Walk back toward the one you turned away from. This is the OT verb for repentance — the same concept as Greek metanoia but even more physical in its imagery. When the prophets cry shuv to Israel, they are not asking for a feeling or a ritual. They are describing a physical picture: you have been walking away from YHWH, turn your body around, and walk back toward Him. The book of Hosea is built entirely on this word — God calling His people to turn around and come home.
H7725.why_mistranslated: English return is primarily about physical location — go back to a place. Hebrew shuv is about direction and relationship — turn around and face the one you turned away from. This is why the prodigal son story works as a picture of repentance — he came to himself and turned around and walked home.
H7725.author: Kahu Phil Stephens
